theme_scores.theme: Scale and variability of tenant fees
theme_scores.justification: DCLG's own survey of 50 agents is described with method (random sample, searched websites) and cross-referenced external surveys (NALS/ARLA Ref 3, Generation Rent Ref 4/6, Shelter Ref 5) give linked, cited figures on fee size and variability, though some EHS stats lack a reference marker.

theme_scores.theme: Weak tenant market power and misaligned incentives
theme_scores.justification: The OFT 2013 market study is named in prose ('Office of Fair Trading found in their 2013 market study') but carries no reference number or link, so it stays uncited; the rest is unevidenced reasoning about incentives.

Only the NLA Q4 2016 survey (Reference 11, 'a quarter of landlords... did not know whether their letting agent charged fees') is properly cited; claims about inconsistent display and double-charging are asserted without supporting data.

theme_scores.theme: Financial and behavioural harm to tenants
theme_scores.justification: EHS 2014-15 figures (60% median fee rise, £223 mean) and Citizens Advice findings (Reference 13: 64% had problems paying, 42% borrowed) are clearly linked to the claim of financial hardship and deterred moves.
EHS 2014/15 (Reference 1) gives figures on sector growth and tenancy length but with little explanation of how this supports the fee problem beyond description.
Descriptive statements about deposits and holding fees carry no citation or data at all.
NLA survey and Citizens Advice (Reference 9: 60% vs 88% fee incidence) are mentioned with some explanation but method detail for the NLA anecdotal claim is thin.
Shelter's 2013 finding (Reference 12: 'one in four... charged unfair fees') is named with a citation but minimal explanation of methodology or how it links to the diagnosis.

reasoning: The diagnosis section is built on four core themes. 'Scale and variability of tenant fees' reaches level 2: DCLG's own agent survey is described methodologically and is reinforced by cited external data (NALS/ARLA Ref 3, Generation Rent Ref 4/6, Shelter Ref 5) showing fee ranges (£30-£780) and median/mean figures, clearly linked to the claim of high, variable fees. 'Financial and behavioural harm to tenants' also reaches level 2, citing EHS 2014-15 (60% median rise) and Citizens Advice (Ref 13: 64% had problems paying, 42% borrowed), directly linked to the harm claim. By contrast, 'Weak tenant market power' stays at level 1: the only evidence, the OFT 2013 market study, is named in prose but never given a reference number or link, so a reader cannot trace it; the rest is argument about incentives, not evidence. 'Failure of existing transparency requirements' also sits at level 1: only the NLA survey (Ref 11) is properly cited, while claims about inconsistent display and double-charging remain unevidenced assertions. The mean of the four core levels (2,1,1,2) is 1.5, which rounds down to 1. A strong counter-example is the 50-agent fee comparison table, which is genuinely linked and quantified, pulling against a low score, but the unlinked OFT citation and uncited 'confusion/double-charging' claims pull the average down. To reach level 2 overall, the document would need to properly cite the OFT study and substantiate the transparency-failure claims with named, traceable sources.
